body_markdown:
Profit and cash arrive at different times. Profit is recorded when you make the sale. Cash shows up later, after the stock has been bought, the customer's credit term has run out and the payment has cleared. That is how a business can report a good month and still struggle to make payroll on the 15th.


It is a common worry. In[research by Visa](https://newsbytes.ph/2025/05/27/visa-eyes-expansion-of-credit-access-to-local-smes/?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) , 44% of small and medium businesses named cash flow as a top issue. This guide explains why the gap opens even in a healthy business, then shows how to measure it with the cash conversion cycle and how to close it.


## **Why profit and cash come apart**


An income statement records a sale when it is made and a cost when it is incurred. Your bank account records only what has been paid. Four situations explain most of the distance between the two.


### **Growth uses cash before it produces any**


Suppose a packaging supplier in Cebu wins a restaurant chain as a client and its monthly orders double. To fill them, it has to buy twice the stock this month, and the chain pays in 60 days. For those two months the supplier carries double the inventory and double the receivables on the same cash it had before. Its sales are at a record while its bank balance is at its lowest.


Seasonal stocking has the same effect. A gift shop that buys inventory in September for the Christmas rush gets that cash back in December and January.


### **Customers pay on terms while suppliers want cash**


Consider a food producer in Bulacan that sells to a supermarket chain on 60-day terms, or on consignment, where it is paid only after the goods sell. Its own suppliers of sugar and packaging expect payment on delivery. Every sale is profitable, yet the producer funds each one out of pocket for two months.


Smaller suppliers have little room to negotiate these terms, a problem the[Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines](https://finex.org.ph/2026/01/30/how-big-business-can-help-smes-grow/?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) has raised with large buyers.


### **Some bills arrive on fixed dates**


Payroll falls on the 15th and the 30th whether or not clients have paid. Thirteenth-month pay must be released[on or before 24 December](https://tribune.net.ph/2026/11/09/dole-reminds-employers-of-deadline-for-13th-month-pay?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) , and the labor department allows no deferments.


Taxes keep their own calendar too. Under the Ease of Paying Taxes Act, VAT on services is[computed on what you billed during the quarter](https://mb.com.ph/2024/3/4/good-news-and-challenges-from-the-bir?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) , no longer on what you collected. A design agency that invoices ₱1 million in March and is paid in May still owes the ₱120,000 in VAT on that invoice in April.


### **Cash leaves without touching profit**


Buying a ₱600,000 delivery van takes ₱600,000 out of the account today. The income statement shows only that year's depreciation, about ₱120,000 if the van is written off over five years. Loan repayments work the same way, because only the interest counts as an expense while the principal comes out of cash without appearing in profit.


The first two situations can be measured in days, and that is the job of the cash conversion cycle.


## **What is the cash conversion cycle?**


The cash conversion cycle (CCC) is the number of days between paying for your stock and collecting cash from the customers who bought it. It adds the days goods sit in inventory to the days customers take to pay, then subtracts the days you take to pay your suppliers.


A shorter cycle means less of your own money is tied up in daily operations. At 55 days, every peso you spend on stock takes about 55 days to come back, and until then the business runs on your reserves or on borrowed money.


## **The cash conversion cycle formula**


**CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO**


Each part of the formula measures a different wait, as the table below shows.


Factor


Days inventory outstanding (DIO)


Days sales outstanding (DSO)


Days payable outstanding (DPO)


What it measures


How long stock sits before it sells


How long customers take to pay you


How long you take to pay suppliers


Formula


Average inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × 365


Average accounts receivable ÷ revenue × 365


Average accounts payable ÷ cost of goods sold × 365


Effect on the cycle


Adds days


Adds days


Subtracts days


Use the same period for every figure: 365 days if your numbers cover a year, or the number of days in the quarter if they cover one. A service business with no stock has a DIO of zero.


## **A worked example in pesos**


Go back to the packaging supplier in Cebu. Last year it recorded ₱12 million in revenue and ₱9 million in cost of goods sold. The table below shows its three calculations.


Factor


DIO


DSO


DPO


Average balance


₱1,110,000 in inventory


₱1,315,000 in receivables


₱740,000 in payables


Divided by


₱9,000,000 cost of goods sold


₱12,000,000 revenue


₱9,000,000 cost of goods sold


Multiplied by 365


45 days


40 days


30 days


**CCC = 45 + 40 − 30 = 55 days**


The business made a gross profit of ₱3 million. Yet at any given time it has about ₱1.69 million of its own money sitting in stock and unpaid invoices, after counting what it still owes suppliers (₱1,110,000 + ₱1,315,000 − ₱740,000). Every day it removes from the collection side frees roughly ₱32,900, which is one day of sales.


## **The days the formula leaves out**


The formula stops counting when the customer pays. That worked when payment meant cash over the counter. More payments are now digital, and a digital payment has two steps: the customer pays, then the funds settle to your account. We explain the mechanics in[how online payments work in the Philippines](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/how-online-payments-work-philippines?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) .


How long the second step takes depends on the payment method and your provider. Standard settlement cycles run from two to seven days. If the Cebu supplier's customers pay by card on day 40 and the funds settle three days later, its real cycle is 58 days.


We see how much those days matter in what merchants ask us. How payouts work is one of the questions we hear most. Partners who serve small neighborhood stores have told us that next-day settlement is too slow for owners who restock daily, and have asked for settlement several times a day. One merchant recently followed up on a payout of about ₱2 million because it had supplier payments due that same week.


The mix of payment methods is also changing how much of this wait a business can remove. QR Ph made up[55% of payment volume on PayMongo](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/midyear-data-drop-2026?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) in the first half of 2026, up from 16% a year earlier. It is the payment method that can be settled instantly, which we cover below.


When you calculate your own cycle, add settlement days to your DSO for the share of sales paid digitally. It gives you a truer number to plan around.


## **How to shorten your cash conversion cycle**


Three changes would cut the Cebu supplier's cycle from 58 days to 28.


### **Collect sooner**


Receivables hold much of the waiting for a business that sells on credit, so start there. Asking for a[downpayment](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/how-to-collect-downpayment-philippines?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) before work begins means part of the invoice is collected on day zero. If the supplier takes 30% when the order is placed and keeps 40-day terms on the balance, its DSO falls from 40 days to 28.


If you offer credit,[set your terms deliberately](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/net-30-credit-terms-philippines?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) and send the invoice on the day you deliver. An invoice that carries a payment link also lets the client pay online as soon as it is approved, without waiting for a check run.


You can create and send invoices with a pay link through


[PayMongo Invoices](https://www.paymongo.com/products/accept-payments/invoices?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) .


[Create an Account](https://dashboard.paymongo.com/signup?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io)


### **Settle sooner**


Check your payout schedule, because the default may not suit how your money moves. All Out Fitness runs gyms alongside an online equipment store, and it used to receive payouts weekly. Jessica, its finance representative,[has said](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/features-all-out-fitness?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) that being able to change the schedule to fit the company's cash needs is what she values in the PayMongo dashboard.


For[QR Ph](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/what-is-qrph?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) payments, PayMongo also offers Instant Settlement, which sends funds to your PayMongo Wallet as soon as the customer pays. It is an add-on that you request.


Activation is subject to our review and approval, and it carries a fee on top of the standard QR Ph rate, shown on our[pricing page](https://www.paymongo.com/en/pricing?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) .


To decide whether the fee is worth paying, price the wait. If the supplier covers shortfalls with a credit line at 2% a month, holding ₱100,000 for three days costs about ₱200. If its own vendor gives 2% off for cash on delivery, having that ₱100,000 three days sooner can be worth ₱2,000. Set the Instant Settlement fee on ₱100,000 of sales against those two figures. For the Cebu supplier, moving its digital payments to QR Ph with Instant Settlement removes the three settlement days.


### **Pay suppliers on your terms**


Paying a supplier early shortens your DPO, which lengthens your cycle. Suppose the Cebu supplier's main vendor allows 45 days and it has been paying at 30 out of habit. Using the full term raises its DPO from 30 days to 45. Pay on the due date all the same, since a supplier who is paid late has little reason to keep extending credit.


Scheduling supplier payments ahead of time lets you hold cash until the day it is due. With[PayMongo Disbursements](https://www.paymongo.com/products/money-movement/disbursements?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) , you can send those payments from your Wallet through InstaPay or PESONet. Our guide to[disbursement in the Philippines](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/disbursement-philippines?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) covers the options.


### **What the changes add up to**


The table below shows the supplier before and after.


Factor


Before


After

45


45

The cycle falls by 30 days, which frees about ₱860,000 that had been tied up in receivables and early supplier payments. Its sales and prices are the same as before.


Inventory is the remaining lever. Ordering slow-moving items in smaller quantities, more often, keeps less cash on the shelf. If the gap is still too wide after these changes,[short-term financing](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/best-loans-small-businesses-ph?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) can cover it.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### ****What is a good cash conversion cycle?****


It depends on the kind of business. A restaurant that is paid at the table and buys ingredients on short credit can run a cycle close to zero. A distributor that holds stock and gives customers 30 to 60 days to pay will run much longer. Compare your number with your own previous quarters and with businesses similar to yours.


#### ****Can the cash conversion cycle be negative?****


Yes. A negative cycle means you collect from customers before you pay your suppliers. Supermarkets often work this way, and so do businesses that take full payment up front. In effect, suppliers are funding your operations, which is a strong position as long as you pay them on time.


#### ****What is the difference between the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle?****


The operating cycle is DIO plus DSO, the time from buying stock to collecting cash. The cash conversion cycle subtracts DPO, so it counts only the days you fund yourself. In the worked example, the operating cycle is 85 days and the cash conversion cycle is 55 days.
